newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S. grains/oilseeds prices seen near bottom - trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. grains/oilseeds prices seen near bottom - trade.

text.p: Falling U.S. grains and oilseeds prices may stabilise soon, disappointing Southeast Asian buyers who have stepped away from the market on expectations of a further fall in U.S. corn and soybean values, regional traders said on Wednesday.
"Prices have come down a long way pretty quickly," a trader in a U.S. commodity house told Reuters. "It's not going to continue its freefall."
"Everybody was in a state of shock at the way prices have come down hard and fast in Chicago. We're due for some consolidation here," a senior dealer in a Western commodity trading company said.
Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) corn and soybean futures have fallen more than $1.00 a bushel since July, prompting many U.S. farmers to store their crops in hopes of a recovery.
The fall in prices has driven Southeast Asian buyers to the sidelines, with the possible exception of Indonesia.
A trader in Jakarta said Indonesian buyers may buy up to 80,000 tonnes of Indian soymeal after it was offered meal at US$290 a tonne C&F, with buyers eyeing $285-$287 a tonne.
"I think there might be orders for about 70,000 to 80,000 tonnes of Indian origin soymeal for January delivery," the trader said.
A good chunk of sales from Taiwan, South Korea and Japan will more than make up for the quiet regional market in Southeast Asia, one trader said.
"I think we're going to see another good week of sales" from those countries, the trader said, adding good crush margins in Europe are also "sucking in a lot of (soy)beans" from the market.
Buyers from Malaysia mulling a purchase of at least two cargoes of soymeal decided to wait for lower prices, Singapore-based dealers said.
"The Malaysians pulled back. Everybody is pretty well-covered up to December so there's no rush. The market has become bearish," a trader in a European commodity company said.
"Why should you buy now and keep, when you know the market's going to go down further?" asked a dealer at a Kuala Lumpur flour mill.
The Malaysians were initially looking for a price of around $290 a tonne C&F, but were now holding out for a lower quotation somewhere below $285 a tonne C&F, traders said.
U.S.-origin soymeal was being quoted in Southeast Asia in a range between $285-$287 a tonne C&F for January/February shipment against a price of around $295-$300 last week, traders said.
Indian-origin meal was being quoted here at around $290-$295 a tonne C&F for January/February shipment from last week's level of $298-$305 a tonne, dealers said.
The corn market was also quiet around the region with Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand well-covered to early 1997, dealers said.
Indonesia has just finished its domestic corn harvest and has bumper stocks, while Malaysia and Thailand have ample supplies of the staple.
Prices in the region reflected lower U.S. values, dealers said.

The price of U.S. corn in Southeast Asia dropped to around $148-$150 a tonne C&F for January/February shipment on board a Panamax vessel against a price of around $150-$152 a tonne C&F for December/January shipment last week.
"The slower farmer selling in the U.S. is going to put a brake on the recent slide in prices," a grains analyst said. "I wouldn't count on it falling further."
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
